resources.string: Sphinx blocks ads and trackers across your whole phone by questioning DNS lookups on the device itself. No remote server, no root. It cannot remove ads served from the same address as the content — YouTube is the honest example.
Questioning DNS requests on this device.
Using the list built into the app: %1$s domains.
Using downloaded lists: %1$s domains. Last updated %2$s.
Lists updated — now questioning with %1$s domains.
That update didn\'t take, so your current list is unchanged. Check the connection and the source addresses, then try again.
List sources — the web addresses Sphinx downloads lists from, one per line. These are the only addresses Sphinx contacts on its own, and only when you tap Update.
None of those addresses can be used — sources must start with https://.
Some addresses were skipped — sources must start with https://.
If a site or app breaks, allowlist its domain here. The domain and everything under it will always be let through, even when a block list covers it.
That doesn\'t look like a domain name.
Domains you block yourself, on top of every downloaded list. A custom entry works exactly like a list entry — the domain and everything under it — and your allowlist still wins over it.

Two rules you can set per app. Exclude: Sphinx never filters the app — the fix for an app that breaks, like a bank or another VPN. Block: the app gets no network at all while Sphinx is on. One honest catch: Android runs the gate one way at a time, so while any app is blocked outright, your other apps connect without DNS filtering — blocking is a lockdown, not a filter setting. Rule changes rebuild the filter when you leave the app list.
Tap an app to set its rule. Only apps that can use the network are listed.

Notifications are off for Sphinx, so its status won\'t appear in your notification shade. The filter still works — this only affects the status display. To allow it later: Settings → Apps → Sphinx → Notifications.

A profile saves your app rules, your allowlist, and your own block entries under one name — Home, Kids, Strict, whatever you call them. The block lists themselves are shared by every profile. While a profile is active, editing those rules edits the profile too — what a profile says is always what it does.
No profile is active — you\'re editing the live rules directly.
No profiles yet. Set your rules the way you like them, then save them as a profile.
Save current rules as a new profile…
Name this profile. Your current rules are saved under it, and it becomes the active profile.
Profile saved — it\'s now the active profile.
That name can\'t be used — it may be taken already, empty, or too long.
Profile switched — the filter now runs those rules.
Profile deleted. Your current rules are unchanged.

If this is on, and Sphinx was running when the phone shut down, Sphinx starts itself after the phone restarts — in the same mode, with the same rules. If you had turned Sphinx off, it stays off. This setting itself is off until you turn it on.
Start Sphinx when the phone turns on

Android\'s battery saver can put apps to sleep — and a sleeping filter filters nothing. If Sphinx ever stops unexpectedly, exempting it here is the usual fix. The choice is yours, in Android\'s own settings; Sphinx never changes it for you. And if the filter does stop, this app shows it as off — it never pretends to be protecting you when it isn\'t.
Sphinx is exempt from battery optimization — Android won\'t put it to sleep in the background.
Sphinx is not exempt from battery optimization — aggressive battery modes can stop the filter.
Couldn\'t open Android\'s battery settings from here.

The most recent lookups Sphinx questioned — kept only in memory on this phone, never sent anywhere, and gone when the app\'s process stops. Recording is on by default so you can see Sphinx working; turn it off any time.
Recording is off. Sphinx is still filtering — it just isn\'t writing anything down.
Nothing questioned yet. Turn Sphinx on and use any app — lookups will show up here.
